new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the final syllable. Stated explicitly for the Olrat variety; for Koro proper the same author gives only the areal statement that essentially all Torres-Banks languages have systematic word-final stress, plus the observation that Koro's diphthong /ɛ͡a/ is realised as a diphthong only in the (word-final) stressed syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said for the modern languages (secondary stress every second syllable leftward is reconstructed only for the penultimate-stressed proto-language, François 2005:451).
new_statements.exceptions: None for Olrat or Koro. (For neighbouring Dorig, François 2005:469 notes a word-internal long /aː/ 'tends to attract word stress'.)
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement in a brief phonology note on a corpus page; no discussion of phrase-level prosody or citation forms. The François 2005 statement is areal and diachronically framed (loss of posttonic vowels made the languages oxytone).
new_statements.identity_note: koro1308 is Glottolog 5.1's language-level node 'Koro-Olrat' grouping two Gaua varieties that François and ISO 639-3 treat as separate languages: Koro (koro1318, ISO krf, c. 250 speakers, villages Kōrō and Biam) and Olrat (olra1234, ISO olr, extinct since 2009). The explicit stress statement ('Stress is word-final') is for OLRAT only, based on François's 2003 work with the last speaker Maten Womal. For KORO proper the sources give only François 2005's areal final-stress statement for 'essentially all' Torres-Banks languages and the Koro-specific remark (p.468) that the diphthong /ɛ͡a/ surfaces only under word stress, exemplified in word-final syllables. François 2005 fn.21 calls Koro 'a dialect of the same language' as Dorig (weta1242), which he describes (p.469) as 'a well-behaved oxytone language'.

sources.note: Sec. 3.1 p.451 (areal, all Torres-Banks lgs incl. Koro and Olrat): 'in essentially all the languages of the area, words are now systematically stressed on their final rather than their penultimate syllable (contra Lynch 2000:77)'. Sec. 5.1.2.2 p.468 (Koro-specific): the diphthong /ɛ͡a/ 'in Koro surfaces as [ɛ͡a] under word stress, and as a monophthong [ɛ] in other contexts', ex. (26) *RapiRapi > KRO rɛβrɛ͡aβ with the diphthong in the final syllable; p.469 neighbouring Dorig called 'a well-behaved oxytone language'.
